newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli-PLO breakthrough, but tough road ahead.
newsitem.headline: Israeli-PLO breakthrough, but tough road ahead.

text.p: The PLO and Israel said on Thursday that the handshake between Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had saved Middle East peace.
But officials who helped bring about the first meeting of the two acknowledged that the sides were still far apart on all major issues.

A day after the landmark meeting, Netanyahu faced the central committee of his right-wing Likud party, which convened on Thursday evening in a meeting previously scheduled to deal with internal party matters.
The handshake threw all else into shadow.

"I did everything so this man could betray me and my friends...What right did he have to go and shake the hand of this killer of children," one member of the hundreds-strong central committee screamed on Israel Radio.
Netanyahu, speaking to Israel's Channel One television before the Likud meeting, said any ministers who opposed his policies would be fired.

"The principle of the continuation of this (peace) process according to our understanding, in the way we are directing it, every minister in the government has to accept it otherwise they will not be ministers in the government," he said.
Asked if he would fire those who did not toe the line, Netanyahu said: "If necessary, yes."
The handshake marked a milestone in the political and psychological life of both Netanyahyu and Arafat.
For Arafat, Netanyahu was a scion of revisionist Zionists bent on colonizing all of pre-1948 Palestine. For Netanyahu, the PLO chief and former guerrilla was a "terrorist".
U.S. and international mediators struggling to keep the 1993 Palestinian self-rule deal alive seized on the symbolism of the meeting as evidence of progress.

"For one thing, it crosses what I would consider a psychological threshold," said U.S. Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross. "If you're going to tackle real issues of substance, you have to develop working relationships," he told Israel Television.
The United States had been urging Netanyahu to meet Arafat since he narrowly beat a centre-left Labour government in May elections.

Netanyahu hesitated, arousing Palestinian fears that he wanted to rewrite the Olso accord that the late Labour prime minister Yitzhak Rabin sealed with a handshake with Arafat on the White House lawn three years ago.
Aides to Arafat and Netanyahu put a positive spin for their domestic audiences on the outcome of the one-hour summit.

Israelis stressed that self-rule in the Gaza Strip and West Bank could not go ahead unless their security needs were satisfied. Palestinians said they had not given in to Israeli demands to modify Oslo, only to discuss its implementation.

Palestinians want implementation of Oslo clauses on an Israeli troop redeployment in Hebron and other areas of the West Bank, opening a passage for Palestinians to travel between the West Bank and Gaza, and easing the closure of Israel's border with those areas.
Both sides agreed to resume talks on Hebron next week but they could bog down as Israel wants to change security arrangements in the city and the Palestinians do not.

"There may be changes to certain elements," said Terje Larsen, the United Nations coordinator who helped engineer the summit. "Israelis may request modifications on certain elements in the agreements but the Palestinians have to approve them, and they have strongly rejected any modifications," he told Reuters.

Larsen seized on what many Israeli commentators saw as a sea change in Israel's right-wing -- the split between the mainstream Likud and the far right Greater Israel camp, which believes in settling the areas as Israel's God-given duty.

"What is important is that the Likud have crossed the psychological barrier by meeting the enemy in a cordial manner and committing itself to a peace accord signed with the PLO, which it has recognised yesterday for the first time," he said.
